lead: On the first full day of Lent the Church puts a choice in front of us. Moses says to Israel, “Choose life.” Jesus says that the way to life passes through the Cross, and that it is walked daily. Psalm 1 draws the same two roads: the tree by the water and the chaff in the wind. Lent is not only about giving something up. It is about which way we are walking.

set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses' last words, spoken in the land of Moab, with the Jordan still to be crossed. Moses himself will not cross it. These verses close his final appeal. Ancient treaties ended with lists of blessings and curses and called witnesses, and Deuteronomy shapes Israel's covenant in a similar way. Other nations called on their gods as witnesses; here it is heaven and earth (v. 19), for Israel has only one God.
str: v. 15: two ways are set out: life and death.
v. 16: the first way: love, walk, keep, and live.
vv. 17–18: the second way: the heart turns away, and you perish.
vv. 19–20: witnesses and the appeal: choose life.
kw: In Deuteronomy God is the one who chooses Israel (7:6–7). Now Israel is asked to choose in return. The covenant has two partners, and the human one is really able to say yes or no.
The same verb is used of a man who “clings to his wife” (Genesis 2:24). Obedience here is more than keeping rules: it is holding on to a person.
More than breathing: length of days, land, children, and above all closeness to God. In v. 20 the Hebrew says literally that he “is your life”; the NRSV gives “that means life to you”.
vv: See, I have set before you today life and prosperity, death and adversity.
“Today” comes four times in this reading. Moses speaks as if the choice were being made at this very moment, and each generation hearing the book read is placed in the same moment.
Choose life so that you and your descendants may live,
God gives the answer to his own question: he tells them what to choose. And the choice reaches beyond the one who makes it, to children not yet born.
loving the Lord your God, obeying him, and holding fast to him;
Here is what choosing life means in practice: three verbs of relationship.
ch: The Catechism says that the way of Christ leads to life and a contrary way leads to destruction, and that the “two ways” have always had a place in the Church's teaching (CCC 1696, citing Deuteronomy 30:15–20). The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings, opens with the words that there are two ways, one of life and one of death. St John Paul II applies Moses' words directly to our time as a call to be unconditionally for life (Evangelium Vitae 28). God made us able to choose, and this is why our choices matter so much (CCC 1730–1733).

set: Peter has just said that Jesus is “the Messiah of God” (9:20). Immediately Jesus tells them what this will mean. This is the first of the announcements of his Passion in Luke. The elders, chief priests and scribes are the groups that made up the leading council in Jerusalem, so he is speaking of the action of certain authorities, and no blame falls on the Jewish people (CCC 597).
str: v. 22: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and be raised.
v. 23: the disciple's way: deny, take up, follow.
vv. 24–25: why: two sayings about losing and saving.
kw: A small Greek word which Luke loves. It does not mean blind fate. It speaks of God's saving plan, which runs through the suffering and comes out at the other side.
The verb which Luke will use when Peter denies Jesus (22:57). Either I deny myself, or I end up denying him.
Only Luke has this word in the saying. It changes the picture: the Cross is no longer one heroic moment, but something to take up again each morning.
vv: “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me.

He speaks “to them all”: this is not only for apostles or martyrs. For his first hearers a cross was a horror, and no one took one up unless they were going to their death. To deny oneself means no longer putting oneself at the centre.
For those who want to save their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will save it.
The Greek word for “life” (psychē) also means the self. A life clutched tight is lost, and a life given away is kept. “For my sake” is the key: it is not loss for its own sake.
What does it profit them if they gain the whole world, but lose or forfeit themselves?
A businessman's question. Where Mark says “life”, Luke says “themselves”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus calls his disciples to “take up their cross and follow him”, for Christ suffered for us leaving an example, and he wants to associate with his sacrifice those who are its first beneficiaries (CCC 618). It also says plainly that taking up one's cross each day and following Jesus is the surest way of penance (CCC 1435). So the daily cross of Lent need not be something unusual. It may be the illness, the difficult relative, the dull duty, accepted with love.

qa: Does Jesus want us to hate ourselves?

No. “Deny themselves” does not mean despising the person God made in his image. It means giving up the claim to be the centre of everything. The saying ends in saving one's life and finding one's true self. The Lord asks for the loss in order to give something greater.
rite: In the Roman calendar 11 February is the commemoration of Our Lady of Lourdes, where Mary appeared to St Bernadette Soubirous in 1858. St John Paul II made this date the World Day of the Sick, first kept in 1993. Today's readings suit the day: the sick who carry their cross daily are often those who teach the rest of us what it means. Today is a good day to visit a sick person or to pray for them.
study: What daily cross are you carrying now? How could you take it up instead of simply putting up with it?
Moses asks you to choose life “today”. Which choice in front of you this week most needs that word?
